summary.text: A Wilf–Zeilberger telescoping certificate—its cleared polynomial identity proved from degree bounds by finite-grid interpolation—turns the binomial sum into the explicit base three-term recurrence, which is then iterated with $2\times2$ transfer matrices and an intermediate term is eliminated to obtain the recurrence for every arithmetic subsequence.  After dividing a matrix-entry polynomial by its forced shifted quadratic factors, the remaining degree-$2m$ polynomial is reflection-symmetric and alternates sign at consecutive half-integers, so it has exactly one real zero in each intervening interval; affine rescaling gives $P$, while applying the same construction at $2m$ and extracting its even part gives $Q$, with the stated symmetry and root intervals (the $m=1$ case follows directly from the explicit quadratics).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a_n=[x^{2n}]\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)^n\qquad(n\geq 0).
\]
Thus \(a_0=1\). Expanding \((1+x)^n(1-x)^{-n}\), and then replacing the summation index \(k\) by \(n-k\), gives, for \(n>0\),
\[
 a_n=\sum_{k=0}^n \binom nk\binom{2n+k-1}{n-1}.                                      \tag{1}
\]
We prove the assertion by first finding a recurrence for \((a_n)\), and then passing to every arithmetic subsequence by transfer matrices.

Put
\[
 p(t)=5t^2-5t+1,
\]
\[
 \alpha(t)=(2t+1)(2t+2)p(t),
 \qquad
 \beta(t)=4(55t^4-34t^2+3).
\]
Notice that
\[
 \alpha(-t)=(2t-1)(2t-2)(5t^2+5t+1).                         \tag{2}
\]
The basic recurrence is
\[
 \alpha(n)a_{n+1}-\alpha(-n)a_{n-1}=\beta(n)a_n
 \qquad(n\geq1).                                             \tag{3}
\]

We first establish (3). For \(n>0\), define
\[
 F(n,k)=\binom nk\binom{2n+k-1}{n-1},
\]
with the convention that a binomial coefficient is zero outside its usual range. Define also
\[
 D(n,k)=n(k-n-1)(k+2n-2)(k+2n-1)
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(n,k)=k\big(&110k^2n^5+30k^2n^4-68k^2n^3-20k^2n^2+6k^2n+2k^2\\
 &+410kn^6-260kn^5-258kn^4+150kn^3+30kn^2-10kn-2k\\
 &+290n^7-265n^6-187n^5+138n^4+33n^3-5n^2-4n\big).
\end{aligned}
\]
Set
\[
 R(n,k)=\frac{S(n,k)}{D(n,k)},\qquad H(n,k)=R(n,k)F(n,k)
\]
whenever the displayed denominator is nonzero. The elementary binomial ratios are
\[
 \frac{F(n,k+1)}{F(n,k)}=
 \frac{(n-k)(2n+k)}{(k+1)(n+k+1)},                            \tag{4}
\]
\[
 \frac{F(n+1,k)}{F(n,k)}=
 \frac{(2n+k)(n+1)(2n+k+1)}{n(n-k+1)(n+k+1)},                \tag{5}
\]
and
\[
 \frac{F(n-1,k)}{F(n,k)}=
 \frac{(n-k)(n+k)(n-1)}{n(2n+k-2)(2n+k-1)}.                 \tag{6}
\]
Substitution of (4)–(6), followed by clearing denominators, gives the polynomial identity
\[
 H(n,k+1)-H(n,k)
 =\alpha(n)F(n+1,k)-\alpha(-n)F(n-1,k)-\beta(n)F(n,k).       \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, the cleared numerator of (7) is obtained by replacing the three ratios respectively by the numerators and denominators in (4), (5), and (6); after collecting powers of \(k\), every coefficient is zero. This is a direct polynomial expansion. One economical way to check the expansion is to note that its degree is at most \(19\) in \(n\) and at most \(12\) in \(k\), and that substitution at the grid \(0\leq n\leq19\), \(0\leq k\leq12\) gives zero; interpolation in each variable then proves that the polynomial is identically zero. Thus (7) is a genuine polynomial identity, not merely an identity at integer arguments.

For integers \(n\geq2\), sum (7) over \(0\leq k<n\). The left side telescopes because \(S(n,0)=0\). The sums involving \(F(n-1,k)\) already contain all the terms of \(a_{n-1}\). The other two sums omit only their top terms. The required endpoint cancellation is
\[
\begin{aligned}
0={}&S(n,n)(2n+1)(2n+2)\\
&+\alpha(n)(n+1)3(3n+1)D(n,n)(2n+2)\\
&+\alpha(n)3(3n+1)(3n+2)D(n,n)\\
&-\beta(n)D(n,n)(2n+1)(2n+2),                               \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
which again follows by direct expansion. Equivalently, after division by the nonzero factors, (8) says precisely that the telescoping endpoint \(H(n,n)\), together with the omitted terms \(F(n,n)\), \(F(n+1,n)\), and \(F(n+1,n+1)\), cancels. Here one uses
\[
\frac{F(n+1,n)}{F(n,n)}=\frac{(n+1)3(3n+1)}{2n+1},
\]
\[
\frac{F(n+1,n+1)}{F(n,n)}=
\frac{3(3n+1)(3n+2)}{(2n+1)(2n+2)}.
\]
Consequently the sum of (7) is exactly (3). For \(n=1\), (3) follows directly from \(a_0=1,a_1=2,a_2=16\). This proves the basic recurrence for every \(n\geq1\).

We now encode (3) by the matrix
\[
 S(x)=\begin{pmatrix}
 \beta(x)&\alpha(-x)\\
 \alpha(x)&0
 \end{pmatrix}.                                               \tag{9}
\]
If \(v_n=(a_n,a_{n-1})^T\), then (3) is equivalent to
\[
 S(n)v_n=\alpha(n)v_{n+1}.                                    \tag{10}
\]
For an integer \(r\geq0\) and a real variable \(x\), let
\[
 T_r(x)=S(x+r-1)S(x+r-2)\cdots S(x),\qquad T_0(x)=I,
\]
and denote its upper-right entry by
\[
 f_r(x)=(T_r(x))_{12}.                                        \tag{11}
\]
All entries here are polynomials. From matrix multiplication,
\[
 f_{r+2}(x)=\beta(x+r+1)f_{r+1}(x)
 +\alpha(-x-r-1)\alpha(x+r)f_r(x),                            \tag{12}
\]
with
\[
 f_0=0,
 \qquad f_1(x)=\alpha(-x).
\]
The polynomials \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) both have degree four, with leading coefficients \(20\) and \(220\), respectively. It follows inductively from (12) that, for \(r\geq1\),
\[
 \deg f_r=4r,
 \qquad \operatorname{lc}(f_r)>0.                            \tag{13}
\]
Indeed, the two summands on the right of (12) both have degree \(4r+8\); their leading coefficients are respectively \(220\operatorname{lc}(f_{r+1})\) and \(400\operatorname{lc}(f_r)\), so they are positive and cannot cancel.

The entry \(f_r\) has several explicit factors. Let
\[
 K_r(x)=\alpha(-x)\prod_{j=1}^{r-2}p(-x-j),                  \tag{14}
\]
where an empty product is \(1\). We claim
\[
 K_r\mid f_r.                                                 \tag{15}
\]
The factor \(\alpha(-x)\) follows immediately by induction from (12). To obtain the remaining factors, let \(s\) be either root of \(p(-s)=0\), namely
\[
 \sigma_1=\frac{-5+\sqrt5}{10},\qquad
 \sigma_2=\frac{-5-\sqrt5}{10}.                             \tag{16}
\]
A direct expansion gives
\[
 \beta(x)\beta(x+1)+\alpha(-x-1)\alpha(x)
 =(5x^2+5x+1)\,4(2440x^6+7320x^5+3813x^4-4574x^3
 -3112x^2+395x+288).                                         \tag{17}
\]
Thus the left side of (17) vanishes whenever \(p(-x)=0\). Applying two consecutive matrices in (9), (17) shows
\[
 f_{j+2}(s-j)=0.
\]
Since also \(p(s+1)=0\), recurrence (12) propagates this zero to every \(f_r\) with \(r\geq j+2\). Therefore both \(\sigma_1-j\) and \(\sigma_2-j\) are roots of \(f_r\), and hence
\[
 p(-x-j)=5(x-(\sigma_1-j))(x-(\sigma_2-j))
\]
divides \(f_r\).

These quadratic factors are pairwise coprime, and they are coprime to \(\alpha(-x)\). Indeed, \(-1<\sigma_1,\sigma_2<0\), and
\[
 \sigma_1-\sigma_2=\frac{\sqrt5}{5}

differs from every integer: if it were an integer \(q\), then \(5q^2=1\), which is impossible. Thus no root \(\sigma_i-j\) of one shifted quadratic can equal a root \(\sigma_{i'}-j'\) of another unless both indices and both roots agree. The roots of
\[
 \alpha(-x)=20(x-	frac12)(x-1)(x-\sigma_1)(x-\sigma_2)
\]
likewise do not meet the shifted roots with \(j\geq1\). This proves (15).

Define the quotient polynomial
\[
 G_r(x)=\frac{f_r(x)}{K_r(x)},                                \tag{18}
\]
so that \(f_r=K_rG_r\). For \(r\geq2\), (13) and (14) give
\[
 \deg K_r=4+2(r-2)=2r,
 \qquad \deg G_r=2r,                                         \tag{19}
\]
and \(G_r\) has positive leading coefficient.

We next locate every root of \(G_r\). The following elementary signs at half-integers are useful. For an integer \(q\),
\[
 p(q/2)=\frac{5(q-1)^2-1}{4};

the only negative value occurs at \(q=1\), and it is never zero. Also
\[
 \alpha(q/2)=(q+1)(q+2)p(q/2),
\]
so \(\alpha(q/2)<0\) exactly for \(q=1\), and it is zero exactly for \(q=-1,-2\). Finally,
\[
 \beta(q/2)<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad q=1\text{ or }q=-1,
\]
and \(\beta(q/2)\ne0\) for every integer \(q\). The last assertion follows on writing
\[
55(q/2)^4-34(q/2)^2+3= rac{55q^4-136q^2+48}{16}:

the numerator is negative at \(q=\pm1\), positive at \(q=0\), and positive for \(|q|\ge2\).

Using this sign table in (12) gives, by strong induction on \(r\),
\[
 f_r(-j/2)\ne0,
 \qquad
 f_r(-j/2)<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad j+1=2r             \tag{20}
\]
for every integer \(r\geq1\) and every integer \(j\geq0\). Here are the details of the induction. The assertions for \(r=1\) follow from \(f_1(x)=\alpha(-x)\). For \(r=2\),
\[
 f_2(x)=\beta(x+1)f_1(x),
\]
and the stated sign follows from the table. For the induction step, evaluate (12) at \(x=-j/2\). The two terms become
\[
 A f_{r+1}(-j/2),\qquad BC f_r(-j/2),
\]
where
\[
 A=\beta\!\left(\frac{2r+2-j}{2}\right),\quad
 B=\alpha\!\left(\frac{j-2r-2}{2}\right),\quad
 C=\alpha\!\left(\frac{2r-j}{2}\right).
\]
The table shows that the first term is negative exactly when \(j+1=2(r+2)\), and otherwise is positive. If \(B\) or \(C\) vanishes, the second term is zero. If neither vanishes, the signs of \(B,C\), together with the two induction hypotheses, show that the second term has the same sign as the first: both are negative at \(j+1=2(r+2)\), and both are positive otherwise. Thus their sum is nonzero and has exactly the sign asserted in (20).

At the same point, (14) reads
\[
 K_r(-j/2)=\alpha(j/2)
 \prod_{k=1}^{r-2}p((j-2k)/2).                               \tag{21}
\]
All factors are nonzero. There is one negative quadratic factor precisely when \(j=2k+1\) for some \(1\leq k\leq r-2\). Combining this observation with the sign of \(\alpha(j/2)\) gives
\[
 K_r(-j/2)<0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 j\text{ is odd and }j+3\leq2r.                             \tag{22}
\]
Since \(f_r=K_rG_r\), (20) and (22) imply, for \(0\leq j\leq2r\),
\[
 G_r(-j/2)<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad j\text{ is odd},  \tag{23}
\]
and none of these values is zero.

Therefore, for each \(j=0,1,\ldots,2r-1\), the values of \(G_r\) at \(-j/2\) and \(-(j+1)/2\) have opposite signs. By continuity there is a root in each open interval
\[
 \left(-\frac{j+1}{2},-\frac j2\right).                     \tag{24}
\]
The intervals are disjoint, so these are \(2r\) distinct real roots. By (19), \(G_r\) has degree \(2r\); hence these are all its complex roots. In particular every root \(u\) of \(G_r\) is real and satisfies
\[
 -r<u<0.                                                      \tag{25}
\]

There is also a reflection identity. Since \(\beta\) is even, direct inspection of (9) gives
\[
 S(-x-1)^T=S(x+1).
\]
Reversing the factors in a product and transposing therefore gives
\[
 T_r(-x-r)^T=T_r(x+1).                                       \tag{26}
\]
Taking the appropriate matrix entries yields
\[
 \alpha(-x)f_r(-x-r)=\alpha(x+r)f_r(x).                      \tag{27}
\]
On the other hand, using \(p(t)=p(1-t)\) and reversing the factors in (14),
\[
 K_r(-x-r)\alpha(-x)=K_r(x)\alpha(x+r).                     \tag{28}
\]
Substituting \(f_r=K_rG_r\) into (27), using (28), and cancelling the nonzero polynomial factors gives the polynomial identity
\[
 G_r(-x-r)=G_r(x).                                            \tag{29}
\]

We now construct the desired polynomials for \(m\geq2\). Define
\[
 P_m(x)=G_m(m(x-1)).                                          \tag{30}
\]
By (19), \(\deg P_m=2m\). Equation (29) gives
\[
 P_m(1-x)=G_m(-mx)=G_m(m(x-1))=P_m(x),                        \tag{31}
\]
so the required symmetry holds. If \(z\in\mathbb C\) is a root of \(P_m\), then \(m(z-1)\) is a root of \(G_m\). All roots of \(G_m\) are the real numbers described by (24), so \(z\) is real. Writing \(u=m(z-1)\), (25) gives
\[
 0<1+u/m<1.
\]
Thus every root of \(P_m\) lies in \((0,1)\), hence in \([0,1]\).

To construct \(Q_m\), consider
\[
 R_m(x)=G_{2m}(m(x-1)).                                      \tag{32}
\]
Using (29) with \(r=2m\),
\[
 R_m(-x)=G_{2m}(-mx-m)=G_{2m}(mx-m)=R_m(x).
\]
Thus \(R_m\) is even. Consequently there is a unique polynomial \(Q_m\) such that
\[
 R_m(x)=Q_m(x^2);                                             \tag{33}
\]
explicitly, if \(R_m(x)=\sum c_i x^i\), then
\[
 Q_m(y)=\sum_i c_{2i}y^i.
\]
Since \(R_m\) has degree \(4m\), (33) shows that
\[
 \deg Q_m=2m.                                                 \tag{34}
\]
If \(z\in\mathbb C\) satisfies \(Q_m(z^2)=0\), then by (33), \(m(z-1)\) is a root of \(G_{2m}\). Such a root is real and lies strictly between \(-2m\) and \(0\). Hence \(z\) is real and
\[
 -1<z=1+\frac{u}{m}<1.
\]
Thus all roots of \(Q_m(x^2)\) are real and belong to \([-1,1]\).

It remains to prove that these polynomials give the required recurrence. Fix \(m\geq2\), and first suppose \(n\geq2\). Iterating (10) through \(m\) consecutive indices gives
\[
 T_m(mn)v_{mn}=A_+v_{m(n+1)},
\quad
 A_+=\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\alpha(mn+i),                          \tag{35}
\]
and
\[
 T_m(m(n-1))v_{m(n-1)}=A_-v_{mn},
\quad
 A_-=\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\alpha(m(n-1)+i).                     \tag{36}
\]
Write
\[
 U=T_m(mn),\qquad F=T_m(m(n-1)).
\]
Eliminating the intermediate coordinate \(a_{mn-1}\) from (35) and (36) gives
\[
 A_-F_{12}A_+a_{m(n+1)}+U_{12}\det(F)a_{m(n-1)}
 =A_-(F_{12}U_{11}+U_{12}F_{22})a_{mn}.                      \tag{37}
\]
This is just the two-by-two determinant identity: multiply the first row of (35) by \(A_-F_{12}\), and use the two rows of (36) to remove \(a_{mn-1}\) and \(a_{m(n-1)-1}\). Also,
\[
 F_{12}U_{11}+U_{12}F_{22}=(UF)_{12},                        \tag{38}
\]
because scalar multiplication is commutative.

The three upper-right entries in (37) are evaluations of the polynomials already constructed:
\[
 F_{12}=f_m(m(n-1))=K_m(m(n-1))P_m(n),                       \tag{39}
\]
\[
 U_{12}=f_m(mn)=K_m(mn)P_m(-n),                              \tag{40}
\]
where (40) uses the reflection (29), and, because concatenating the two products gives \(UF=T_{2m}(m(n-1))\),
\[
 (UF)_{12}=f_{2m}(m(n-1))
 =K_{2m}(m(n-1))Q_m(n^2).                                   \tag{41}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \det S(x)=-\alpha(x)\alpha(-x),

tso
\[
 \det F=(-1)^m A_-
 \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\alpha(-m(n-1)-i).                        \tag{42}
\]

We record the elementary product identities that normalize (37). Since
\[
 \alpha(x)=(2x+1)(2x+2)p(x),
\]
pairing the consecutive linear factors gives
\[
 A_+=\left(\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn+k)\right)
       \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}p(mn+i).                             \tag{43}
\]
The symmetry \(p(x)=p(1-x)\), with the reindexing \(j=i+m-1\), gives
\[
 \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}p(mn+i)
 =\prod_{j=m-1}^{2m-2}p(-m(n-1)-j).                          \tag{44}
\]
Comparing (14) for \(m\) and \(2m\), equations (43)–(44) imply
\[
 K_m(m(n-1))A_+
 =K_{2m}(m(n-1))\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn+k).                    \tag{45}
\]
Similarly, expanding all \(\alpha(-m(n-1)-i)\), joining the two consecutive blocks of \(p\)-factors, and pairing their linear factors gives
\[
 K_m(mn)\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\alpha(-m(n-1)-i)
 =K_{2m}(m(n-1))\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn-k).                    \tag{46}
\]
These identities are simply equalities between the same products after reindexing; no roots or divisions are involved.

Insert (39)–(46) into (37). Every term has the common factor
\[
 A_-K_{2m}(m(n-1)).
\]
For \(n\geq2\) this factor is nonzero: all arguments of \(\alpha\) in \(A_-\) are nonnegative integers, where neither the linear factors nor \(p\) vanish, and the factors of \(K_{2m}(m(n-1))\) likewise do not vanish because \(p\) has no integral root. Cancelling it yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left(\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn+k)\right)P_m(n)a_{m(n+1)}\\
&\quad+(-1)^m\left(\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn-k)\right)P_m(-n)a_{m(n-1)}
 =Q_m(n^2)a_{mn}.                                            \tag{47}
\end{aligned}
\]

The case \(n=1\) must be treated separately because the backward product begins at zero and its determinant vanishes. The second term in (47) itself vanishes, since the factor with \(k=2m\) in \(\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2m-k)\) is zero. We need therefore show
\[
 \left(\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2m+k)\right)P_m(1)a_{2m}=Q_m(1)a_m. \tag{48}
\]
This follows from the same two adjacent transfer products without dividing by their determinant. Indeed, iterate (10) from the initial vector \((a_0,a_{-1})\) in the harmless form \((1,-4)^T\): the first multiplication uses \(\alpha(-0)=\alpha(0)=2\) and produces the correct forward relation, while the zero determinant at the initial point forces the two columns of the backward product to satisfy
\[
 F_{12}a_{m-1}=F_{22}a_m.
\]
Using this relation to eliminate the middle coordinate from the forward product gives
\[
 f_m(0)\left(\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\alpha(m+i)\right)a_{2m}
 =f_{2m}(0)a_m.                                               \tag{49}
\]
Now write \(f_m(0)=K_m(0)G_m(0)\) and \(f_{2m}(0)=K_{2m}(0)G_{2m}(0)\). Here \(G_m(0)=P_m(1)\) and \(G_{2m}(0)=Q_m(1)\). The specialization of the product identity (45) at \(n=1\) says
\[
 K_m(0)\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\alpha(m+i)
 =K_{2m}(0)\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2m+k).
\]
All the remaining factors are nonzero, so (49) reduces to (48). Thus (47) holds for every \(n\geq1\).

Finally consider \(m=1\), which is best kept separate. Take
\[
 P_1(x)=5x^2-5x+1,
 \qquad
 Q_1(y)=4(55y^2-34y+3).
\]
Both have degree two, \(P_1(x)=P_1(1-x)\), and recurrence (47) is exactly the already proved basic recurrence (3). The roots of \(P_1\) are
\[
 \frac{5\pm\sqrt5}{10},
\]
so they are real and lie in \((0,1)\). If \(Q_1(z^2)=0\), put \(w=z^2\). Then
\[
 55w^2-34w+3=0,

tso
\[
 w=\frac{17\pm2\sqrt{31}}{55}.
\]
Both values are strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). Hence \(z^2\) is a positive real number. Writing \(z=u+iv\), the reality of \(z^2\) gives \(2uv=0\); if \(u=0\), then \(z^2=-v^2\leq0\), a contradiction, so \(v=0\). Thus \(z\) is real and \(|z|<1\).

For every \(m\geq1\), therefore, the polynomials \(P=P_m\) and \(Q=Q_m\) have degree \(2m\), satisfy the recurrence in the statement for \(b(n)=a_{mn}\), obey \(P(x)=P(1-x)\), have every zero of \(P\) in \([0,1]\), and have every zero of \(Q(x^2)\) real and in \([-1,1]\), as required.
